did.abstract: Gary M. Olson is a professor emeritus of psychology and information at the University of Michigan. His research focuses on how information technology can be used to support work when participants are in different locations. This collection documents Olson's research and professional work, primarily that done at the University of Michigan, from 1986-2003. Included are administrative records, subject files, publications, meeting materials, and other records relating to various projects in which Olson was involved. Also included are Olson's files relating to the reshaping of U-M's School of Information.

bioghist.p: Gary M. Olson received his BA from the University of Minnesota in 1967, and his MA and PhD in psychology from Stanford University in 1968 and 1970, respectively. Following service in the U.S. Naval Reserve from 1970 to 1973, he served two years on the faculty of Michigan State University. Olson joined the faculty in University of Michigan Department of Psychology in 1975, earning the rank of professor in 1984. From 1984 to 1995, Olson served at the director of the Cognitive Science and Machine Intelligence Laboratory (CSMIL), a joint venture of the School of Business Administration, the College of Engineering, and the College of Literature, Science and the Arts. He joined the University of Michigan School of Information (UMSI) as professor and as associate dean for research in 1995.

Olson was the founding director of the Collaboratory for Research in Electronic Work and oversaw its migration from the Office of the Vice President to UMSI. As associate dean, he was instrumental in reshaping the school after its change in scope and mission in 1996, leading to the revitalization of the doctoral program, expansion of the base of externally funded research, and the development of the human-computer interaction specialization. From 1998 to 1999 he served as acting dean of UMSI. He was named the Paul M. Fitts Collegiate Professor of Human-Computer Interaction in 2001.

Olson has published more than 120 articles and book chapters and is the leading authority on how information technology can be used to support work when participants are in different locations. With his wife Judith S. Olson, he co-authored the book Working Together Apart: Collaboration over the Internet (Morgan & Claypool, 2014). In 2006, he was awarded — jointly with Judith S. Olson — the CHI Lifetime Achievement Award from the Special Interest Group on Computer-Human Interaction of the Association for Computing Machinery. The award acknowledged his leadership and lifetime impact on the field of human-computer interaction and contributions to the development of the science of collaboration. Additional recognitions include being named an Association for Psychological Science Fellow (2009) for his work in the cognitive field and an American Psychological Association Fellow (2010). He received the SIGCHI Lifetime Service Award in 2016.

Olson retired from U-M in 2008, moving to the University of California, Irvine, as the Donald Bren Professor of Information and Computer Science. In 2016, he retired from that position but remained active in research.

scopecontent.p: The Gary M. Olson papers documents Olson's research and professional work, primarily that done at the University of Michigan. Included are administrative records, subject files, publications, meeting materials, and other records relating to various projects in which Olson was involved. These projects include the Experimental Research in Electronic Submission (EXPRES) project, the Upper Atmospheric Research Collaboratory (UARC), the Waterford Project, as well as Olson's work on networked multidisciplinary research collaboration more generally. Also included are Olson's files relating to the reshaping of the School of Information at the University of Michigan.

bioghist.p: During the mid 1980s, Gary Olson participated in the Experimental Research in Electronic Submission (EXPRES) project to help improve the communication between researchers across the country. The project was led at Michigan by Daniel E. Atkins. Atkins served as the dean at the School of Information and an associate dean at the College of Engineering. His work at the university encompassed many projects that looked to make scientific research a more collaborative process. The National Science Foundation (NSF) provided funding for the EXPRES project, hoping to use the application as a way to submit and review grant proposals electronically. In June 1986, NSF asked for proposals to create the EXPRES application, which were awarded to the Carnegie Mellon University and the University of Michigan.

Beyond electronic submission, the EXPRES project aimed to enable researchers to collaborate in an electronic environment. Before the creation of electronic communication standards and software applications of this nature, it was difficult to electronically share research with colleagues because of the limitations in the hardware, software, and network environments and the differences among universities and their computer mainframe systems. Through the use of the EXPRES software application, improvements in micro and mainframe computing, and improvements in communication via the Internet, knowledge sharing in an electronic format became an easier process.

In several ways, the EXPRES application was ahead of its time. While it did not fully succeed, it identified many of the issues which were overcome with new technologies. According to Science magazine and NSF, for a couple of years the project managed a "few hundred proposals ... before NSF officials realized that they had bitten off more than they could chew".[1] EXPRES's challenges included "hard-to-use software, balky transmission lines, and incompatibility with existing systems."[2] The average computer user at the time was not able to use EXPRES. In the mid 1990s, NSF tried a different application called FastLane, which though smaller, was a more manageable system for researchers to use. FastLane was used by NSF for submission and review of proposals until January 2023.

Notes:
1) Jeffery Mervis, "NSF Moves Into FastLane to Manage Flow of Grants," Science 267 (1995): 166-167. 2) Ibid.

scopecontent.p: The Meetings and Reports (1 linear ft.) series, spanning 1986-1988, has been sorted chronologically. It contains the project proposal to the NSF. It also contains several files about various site visits taken to Carnegie Mellon, Cambridge, and the NSF. Electronic mail (printed out) correspondence is in this series. Also in this series are technical reviews, project plans, and meeting minutes of the development team.

This series consists of reports, meeting materials, data, manuals and software documentation, and administrative files related to the Upper Atmospheric Research Collaboratory. A copy of the original NSF grant proposal is included.

bioghist.p: The Upper Atmospheric Research Collaboratory was an NSF-funded multidisciplinary initiative to develop a new form of computer and communications technology to enable collaborative research over wide-area networks. Led by Daniel E. Atkins and Gary Olson, this technology enabled researchers from five separate institutions to remotely conduct experiments using data from Sondrestrom Upper Atmospheric Research Facility in Sondre Stromfjord, Greenland.

bioghist.p: The Waterford Project was a collaborative initiative to develop a vaccine for the AIDS virus, led by Robert Gallow (discoverer of the HIV virus and former director of the Institute of Human Virology). The project utilized broadband technology to link Gallo's lab with other researchers at Harvard and the University of California, San Francisco.

scopecontent.p: This series consists of meeting materials, administrative files, project overviews and plans, and supplemental literature regarding the Waterford Project. Also included are records regarding the International Cancer and AIDS Research and Education Net (ICARE Net), an early iteration of this project.
